headline: Toriaezu is 取り (tori, “taking”) plus 敢えず (aezu), from the negative form of 敢ふ (afu, “to bear, endure”).
ホール covers “hall”, “hole” and “whole”, and the source borrows all three from English.
Ichijirushii began as ichishirushi, 逸 (ichi-, “very”) plus 著し (shirushi), and shirushi was voiced to jirushi by rendaku in the Muromachi period.
In sōgō, 総 is a daiyōji replacing 綜.
Sashidasu is 差す (sasu) plus 出す (dasu).
ゲスト is from English guest.
Toku, “to unfasten”, is a doublet of 説く (toku) and 溶く (toku).
Ayatsuru may be 綾 (aya, “thread”) plus 取る (toru, “to take”).
Eki, “liquid”, is from Middle Chinese 液 (yek, “liquid”).
Kokoromi is the continuative stem of the verb 試みる (kokoromiru, “to try, attempt”).
ノイローゼ is from German Neurose.
Tomi is the continuative stem of the verb 富む (tomu, “to be rich”).
Sazukeru derives from the classical verb 授く (sazuku), and a surface analysis suggests さ (sa) plus 付ける (tsukeru).
Kagō is 化 (ka, “change into”) plus 合 (gō, “combine”).
スタート is borrowed from English start.
Seijō is from Middle Chinese 正常.
Shujinkō is from Middle Chinese 主人公 (MC tsyuX nyin kuwng).
アンコール is borrowed from English encore.
Uttae is the continuative stem of the verb 訴える (uttaeru).
Chokkan is cognate with 直観.
Neiro is 音 (ne, “tone; sound”) plus 色 (iro, “colour”), and the source compares German Klangfarbe, “sound-color”.
In rikutsu, 屈 is a daiyōji replacing 窟, and the source traces it to Liu Yiqing's A New Account of the Tales of the World.
Nomikomu is 飲み (nomi, the stem of 飲む (nomu, “to drink; to swallow”)) plus 込む (komu, “to go into”).
In tokushū, 集 is a daiyōji replacing 輯.
Tamotsu is 手 (ta, “hand”, bound apophonic form) plus 持つ (motsu, “to hold”).
Ha, “blade”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa, and is cognate with 歯 (ha, “tooth”).
マイナス is from English minus.
Yubisasu is 指 (yubi, “finger”) plus 差す (sasu, “to extend”).
Saegiru is a shift from older さいぎる, itself from さきぎる (sakigiru), 先 (saki, “in front”) plus 切る (kiru, “cut”).
Kogitte is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 切手 (kitte, “postage stamp”), with kitte voiced to gitte by rendaku.
Sodachi is the continuative stem of the verb 育つ (sodatsu, “to be raised, to grow up”).
